newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Mandela's island jail to reveal its secrets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mandela's island jail to reveal its secrets.

text.p: Like the torturers and assassins seeking absolution from South Africa's post-apartheid Truth Commission, Robben Island has begun to reveal its role as the country's foremost political prison.
The flat, sandy island in Cape Town's picturesque Table Bay was the Gulag of apartheid's repressive system in an Alcatraz setting which made escape impossible.

On Wednesday, it was handed over to the control of the Department of Arts and Culture, which plans to develop a human rights museum in the cellblock where Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in jail.

"Robben Island was without question the harshest, most iron-fisted outpost in the South African penal system," Mandela, South Africa's president since the first all-race elections in 1994, wrote in his autobiography, "Long Walk to Freedom".
"It was a hardship station not only for the prisoners, but for the prison staff," he said.

In fact, most of the prison staff did not find life on the quiet island much of a hardship. Five nautical miles from Cape Town's glitzy waterfront restaurants and bars, the island held charms for some.
"It's a heartsore business. I enjoyed my work and I enjoyed my time off here on the island," said prison warder Harry Child, who had lived most of his 44 years on Robben Island.
"I think they are wrong to close this prison. I don't want to go and nor does my wife."
GREW UP ON ISLAND
Child was raised on the island, attending the tiny primary school to which he sent his own sons decades later. Following in his father's footsteps, he joined the prison service at 17.
"The fishing, the people, the rough seas, the quietness. There are so many things I will miss," he said as he checked the empty rooms of his small public works department house.
"They most probably got their reasons for closing down the prison and that, but I don't think it's right," he said.
Child's sons Wayne and Jonathan rejoiced at the prospect of leaving their life of isolation, but his wife Josie just cried.
"It's been a wonderful life here. I'm going to miss my house, I'm going to miss my friends, everything," she said.
Minister of Correctional Services Sipo Mzimela signed over control of the island to Minister of Arts, Culture, Science and Technology Lionel Mtshali before Christmas.
The transfer, ending Robben Island's 300-year history as a place of misery, became effective at midnight on December 31.

Ever since the Royal Navy first marooned a troublesome sailor there in the 16th century, successive colonial governments have used Robben Island as a place of banishment for their opponents and social outcasts.
It has been a leper colony, a lunatic asylum and a debtors' prison and all these phases will be reflected in the museum planned for the sandstone cellblock where Mandela lived.
Ahmed Kathrada, appointed by Mandela to oversee the post-prison development of the island on which they formed a lifelong friendship, said in an interview it would be developed as "a site museum".

Though tourists would be given access, the island would be preserved largely as it is now with a village, in which staff lived a near to normal country life, and a prison where political opponents of white rule were contained behind high walls that denied them even a view of Table Mountain.
"MESSAGE OF TRIUMPH AND HOPE"
"The harshness and suffering of prisoners has to be reflected, but the main message of this island should not emphasise suffering, it should be a message of triumph and of hope," said Kathrada.
Much of the history being revealed by apartheid's servants to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission is likely to be reflected in the island museum.

In much the same way that Tutu's truth probe is designed to cement reconciliation between South Africa's former white rulers and the black majority to whom they denied a voice, the island museum will seek to heal the wounds of apartheid's often brutal implementation by revealing the details kept hidden by generations of white overlords.
Fine points of the development will be worked out by a Robben Island Commission in consultation with former prisoners, tourism officials and nature conservationists.

At present, barely a third of the island is occupied. Endangered Jackass penguins have established their most important breeding colony on the sheltered eastern shore and the island includes important nesting sites for a number of species of seabirds.

Das Basson is among the handful of veterans who have found a new life on the prison island. After 24 years spent ferrying prisoners and their vistors back and forth, he will stay on as a ferry skipper for visitors to the museum.
"I've been on the island now for 26 years and I have been working on the boats for 24 years. I started as a deckhand and I worked my way up to a Class Six skipper.
"I've enjoyed it very much. No hassles like in Cape Town. There was a very good spirit, like in any small town. You now everybody and everybody's problems," he said.
Basson acknowledged that history had surprised him.

"I worked with Mr Mandela. I brought him over on the boats quite a few times. When I came here, I was quite a young guy and they (the prisoners) were saying to us: One day we are going to be in charge of this country.
"We'd say: No, no ways, it will never happen. Well, it happened and it's alright, it's okay. No problems," he said.
